For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. DOCUMENT:
Incident Report: Partial Racking Collapse, Aisle 14
Daventry Distribution Centre, Health, Safety and Operations, 18 September 2026

1. Summary of the incident
At 02:47 on 3 September 2026, a reach truck reversing out of aisle 14 struck the front upright of bay 14-22. The upright buckled, and two adjacent bays of pallet racking (14-22 and 14-23) partially collapsed, bringing down 46 pallets of ambient grocery stock from levels 2 to 5. The aisle was unoccupied apart from the driver, who was uninjured. The area was cordoned off within ten minutes and the night shift manager stopped all work in aisles 13 to 15.

2. Immediate response
A racking inspector attended at 07:30 and confirmed that the damage was confined to the two bays. Damaged stock was removed under supervision over the following two days, and the replacement uprights and beams were fitted on 9 September. The aisle reopened on 10 September after a full inspection.

3. Losses
Of the 46 pallets brought down, 18 were written off entirely, at an average stock value of £2,400 per pallet, a loss of £43,200. The remaining 28 pallets were partially damaged, with an average loss after re-sorting of £650 per pallet, a further £21,800. Racking repair and inspection cost £14,800. Total direct cost of the incident was therefore £79,800, excluding lost productivity in aisles 13 to 15 for the six days the area was restricted.

4. Investigation
The driver, employed through our labour agency, had worked at the site for five weeks and held a valid reach-truck licence. CCTV shows the truck reversing at an angle and at a speed the investigating manager judged to be within site limits, before the rear of the truck contacted the upright. The driver stated he was looking over his shoulder at the time but that the upright was obscured by a pallet overhanging the adjacent bay.

The site racking inspection log shows that the upright at 14-22 had been recorded as amber damage (a dent requiring repair within four weeks, with the bay offloaded if not repaired) during the inspection of 2 July, nine weeks before the collapse. No repair or offloading had been carried out. The log also shows 14 other amber items across the site that are past their four-week repair deadline.

5. Protection measures
In 2025 we fitted steel rack-end and upright protectors to aisles 1 to 8. Since then, aisles 1 to 8 have logged 3 reported racking strikes, compared with 19 in aisles 9 to 16. Protectors clearly prevent racking strikes, and fitting them to aisles 9 to 16 would be expected to reduce strikes there by a similar proportion. Aisles 1 to 8 hold slow-moving reserve stock and account for about a fifth of reach-truck movements on site.

6. Root cause
The investigation concludes that the root cause was driver error: an inexperienced agency driver reversing without a clear line of sight. Contributing factors were the overhanging pallet in bay 14-21 and the absence of upright protectors in aisle 14.

7. Actions
7.1 All agency reach-truck drivers to complete an additional site-specific practical assessment, including reversing in aisles, before working unsupervised. Owner: Training Manager. Due: 30 October.
7.2 Fit upright protectors to aisles 9 to 16, at an estimated cost of £22,000. Owner: Facilities Manager. Due: 30 November.
7.3 Reinforce the pallet overhang check in the put-away procedure and include it in team briefings. Owner: Night Shift Manager. Due: immediately.
7.4 Share this report with the labour agency and request a review of how drivers are assessed before placement.

8. Conclusion
This was a serious incident that could have caused injury. With retraining of agency drivers and protectors in the remaining aisles, we are satisfied that the risk of recurrence has been addressed and that normal operations can continue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "with an average loss after re-sorting of £650 per pallet, a further £21,800" -- 28 pallets x £650 = £18,200, not £21,800. The total direct cost should therefore be £43,200 + £18,200 + £14,800 = £76,200, not £79,800.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Protectors clearly prevent racking strikes, and fitting them to aisles 9 to 16 would be expected to reduce strikes there by a similar proportion." -- The comparison is confounded: the document notes aisles 1 to 8 hold slow-moving stock and see only about a fifth of reach-truck movements, so far fewer strikes would be expected there regardless. Protectors also mitigate damage from strikes rather than prevent them. The data do not show protectors cause fewer strikes.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "The investigation concludes that the root cause was driver error" -- The report's own evidence shows the upright had been logged as amber damage nine weeks earlier and was neither repaired nor offloaded, and that 14 other amber items are overdue. The failed inspection-repair process is a direct contributing cause and live site-wide risk, yet the root cause, actions and conclusion that recurrence risk 'has been addressed' never address it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Incident Report, Partial Racking Collapse, Aisle 14

## Overall assessment

The report records the incident clearly, but its central conclusions don't hold up against its own evidence. The cost figure has an arithmetic error. The root cause leaves out the most significant finding in the investigation. The data cited for the protectors doesn't support the conclusion drawn from it. And the statement that normal operations can safely continue is undermined by a site-wide problem the report found and then didn't act on.

## 1. The cost figure is wrong

Section 3: 28 pallets × £650 = **£18,200**, not £21,800.

The corrected total is £43,200 + £18,200 + £14,800 = **£76,200**, not £79,800. The figure was presented as "firm," so this needs correcting before circulation.

The figures are also described as reconciled "against stock records," but they are built from average values per pallet. Either show the reconciliation or describe the figures as estimates.

## 2. The root cause omits the pre-existing damage

Section 4 says upright 14-22 was logged as **amber damage on 2 July**. The rule was to repair it within four weeks or offload the bay. Nine weeks later it had been neither repaired nor offloaded.

A previously damaged, fully loaded upright is a likely reason why one reversing strike, at a speed judged within limits, led to a two-bay collapse. Yet Section 6 doesn't mention it as either a root cause or a contributing factor. Calling the root cause "driver error" is hard to defend when:

- the driver was licensed and travelling within site speed limits;
- his view was blocked by an overhanging pallet the site failed to catch; and
- the structure he hit was already known to be compromised.

The more defensible root cause is a **failure of the racking damage management process**. Driver actions and the overhang were the triggers.

## 3. Fourteen other overdue amber items are left open

Section 4 notes **14 other amber items past their repair deadline**. No action addresses them, and no action addresses why the repair-or-offload process failed.

This directly contradicts the conclusion that "the risk of recurrence has been addressed and normal operations can continue." At minimum, the report needs:

- an immediate action to offload or repair all overdue amber locations, with an owner and a date;
- an investigation into why the July finding wasn't actioned (who owned it, how it was escalated, whether there was a resourcing problem); and
- a control to stop this recurring, such as tracking overdue items with automatic offload or escalation.

## 4. The protector evidence doesn't show what's claimed

- **It isn't before-and-after data.** The author describes it that way, but Section 5 compares two groups of aisles over the same period. There is no "before" figure for aisles 1–8.
- **The groups aren't comparable.** Aisles 1–8 hold slow-moving reserve stock and see about a fifth of reach-truck movements. If strikes are scaled to traffic, aisles 1–8 have about 3 ÷ 0.2 = 15 per unit of traffic, against 19 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 24 for aisles 9–16. That is roughly a 37% difference, not 84%. Different stock types, pick patterns and congestion could account for much of that gap.
- **Protectors don't prevent strikes.** They absorb impacts and reduce damage to uprights. A lower count of *reported* strikes could simply mean strikes on protectors aren't being logged.
- **No time period is given** for the strike counts.

Protectors are still a sensible measure. But the report should justify them as reducing the consequences of strikes, not claim that "protectors clearly prevent racking strikes" or that they will cut strikes "by a similar proportion."

## 5. The other actions are weak or incomplete

- **7.1** retrains agency drivers only. The evidence (licensed driver, speed within limits, blocked view) doesn't single out agency status. Five weeks' experience may be relevant, but it's an assumption here, not a finding. Consider whether permanent drivers have also struck racking.
- **7.3** "Reinforce… and include in team briefings" is not a control. The report doesn't say who put away the overhanging pallet in 14-21, why existing checks missed it, or how overhangs will be detected in future.
- **7.4 has no owner and no due date.** That contradicts the claim that all actions have named owners and dates. "Share and request a review" is also weaker than the author's description of having "involved the agency."
- **No action covers the damage inspection process** (see sections 2 and 3 above).

## 6. Claims not supported in the document

- The author says the **shift manager was interviewed**. The report contains no account of that interview.
- The author says the racking was **independently inspected**. The report says only "a racking inspector," without saying whether it was an internal or external SEMA-approved inspector.
- The driver's speed was "judged" from CCTV by the investigating manager. If speed matters to the conclusion, say how it was measured.

## 7. Minor points

- The aisle was restricted from 3 to 10 September. That is about seven days, not six. Check the figure.
- Today is 13 November, so 7.1 (due 30 October) is overdue unless it has been completed. If this report is still being circulated, it should include an action status update.

## Recommended changes

1. Correct the arithmetic: £18,200 partial-damage loss and £76,200 total.
2. Revise the root cause to name the unactioned amber damage and the failed repair-or-offload process.
3. Add immediate actions for the 14 overdue amber items, plus a process fix, each with an owner and date.
4. Restate the protector justification and remove the "proven" and "prevent strikes" claims.
5. Give 7.4 an owner and date, and strengthen 7.3 into a real control.
6. Withdraw the statement that operations can safely continue until the overdue amber items are resolved.
